newsitem.title: USA: Scientists cast doubt on $10 billion fusion reactor.
newsitem.headline: Scientists cast doubt on $10 billion fusion reactor.

text.p: A $10 billion international effort to build a huge experimental fusion reactor could be derailed by faulty calculations, researchers said in an article released on Thursday.

The proposed International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER), considered the best chance to show that fusion can be a reliable and efficient power source, may not work with its current design, according to an article published in the journal Science.

The project sponsored by the United States, Russia, Europe and Japan is to be completed by 2010. The donut-shaped facility is to be threaded with spiraling magnetic fields that will hold super-hot ions long enough for them to fuse, and become a self-sustaining fusion burn.

But experts from the University of Texas at Austin have warned ITER scientists that the project will not work because turbulance within the building-sized reactor could greatly reduce the amount of energy produced.

The scientists -- William Dorland and Micheal Kotschenreuther -- have warned that turbulence could shorten energy confinement time in ITER "to the point where, far from generating the 1.5 billion watts in fusion power that ITER's official documents project, it may give back no more than a few times the energy used to heat the plasma in the first place," the article said.
That would be too little energy to ignite a fusion burn, the scientists contend.
Because of its large size, the ITER would be more prone to turbulence than smaller existing facilities on which ITER's optimistic projections were based, the article said.
"Our position is that their work, although solid, is not completed yet," Anne Davies, director of the U.S. Energy Department's Office of Fusion Energy, told Reuters.
"I have not been convinced that this is correct. We're not sure that the modelling work is completed yet," she said.
Davies said the ITER plans still have to undergo extensive reviews, and said it was far too early to say whether the scientists raised problems that could push back the project's timetable.
